questions.stem: The right to equality before the law is guaranteed by which Article of the Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: Art 14 — 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' 'Equality before the law' is a British concept from Dicey's rule of law; 'equal protection of laws' is from the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution. Art 12 defines the 'State' for Part III purposes.

questions.stem: Article 19 guarantees citizens how many freedoms (in the current Constitution)?
questions.explanation: Six freedoms after the 44th Amendment (1978): speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession. The 'right to property' was originally the seventh freedom under Art 19(1)(f) but was removed and converted into an ordinary legal right under Art 300A. All six freedoms apply only to citizens, not foreigners.

questions.explanation: Art 21 — 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' Expanded by the Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi (1978) to require the procedure to be fair, just and reasonable. Later readings have recognised the right to privacy (2017 Puttaswamy), clean environment, shelter, livelihood, dignity, and education. Art 21A (86th Amendment) separately guarantees free compulsory education for children aged 6-14.

questions.stem: Which Article gives the right to constitutional remedies, described by Dr Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Art 32 allows any person to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and empowers the Court to issue writs for that purpose. Art 226 gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction (FRs + any other legal right) but the remedy itself is not a fundamental right. Art 136 is the SC's special leave jurisdiction. Art 32 cannot be suspended except during a National Emergency.

questions.stem: The five 'writs' available under Article 32 are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and:
questions.explanation: Five writs: Habeas Corpus ('produce the body' — against unlawful detention), Mandamus (order a public official to do his duty), Prohibition (stop a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction), Certiorari (quash an illegal order of a lower court), Quo Warranto (by what authority — question a person's right to a public office). Injunctions, subpoenas and stays are ordinary civil remedies, not constitutional writs.

questions.stem: The Right to Education was added as Article 21A by which Constitutional Amendment?
questions.explanation: 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Art 21A — free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 as a Fundamental Right. It was operationalised by the Right to Education Act, 2009. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A); 73rd (1992) added Panchayati Raj (Part IX); 44th (1978) tightened the Emergency provisions.

questions.stem: In the landmark Puttaswamy case (2017) the Supreme Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right, flowing primarily from:

options.option_text: Article 21 and other freedoms in Part III

questions.explanation: K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — a nine-judge bench held, unanimously, that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Art 21, and forms part of the freedoms guaranteed in Part III. It overruled earlier contrary precedents (M.P. Sharma 1954, Kharak Singh 1962). The case arose out of challenges to the mandatory linking of Aadhaar.
